en: One should not fear, nor deliberate, nor listen to the words of the opponent; those who desire victory in assemblies must respond instantly.
Absence of agitation, lack of embarrassment, contempt for the opponent,
laughter, and praise of the king— these five are the causes of victory.
If the mediator is unlearned, one should shout loudly that he must be defeated;
if he is learned, let partiality be applied toward him alone. (NKv 3)

*VAR. 3b: udghoṣya; ed: udghuṣya (L) Greed is the reason, wealth is the probandum, and the domestic priest is the example; self-exaltation is the conclusion—this is the procedure for inferences. (NKv 4)
One who desires to know reality should practice for a long time while feeling shame;
one who desires victory should cast aside modesty and raise a great clamor. NKv_5 //
Through teaching and the composition of treatises, one indeed attains renown;
yet whether such authentic proficiency arises at the end of one's life or not remains uncertain.
Who on the surface of the earth will become the praisers of a fool?
If he does not praise himself by himself, when indeed will his peace of mind come to be? (NKv 7)
"The time for verbal expression has passed; it will become clear further on"—for those who teach in this manner, where does the difficulty lie in the text? (NKv 8)
Lack of understanding, excessive faith, and satisfaction with a mere semblance of knowledge—
these three qualities of a disciple arise from the good fortune of a foolish teacher.
If the intellect does not succeed at all in any field of knowledge whatsoever,
then we shall become mantra-practitioners, or yogins, or even ascetics.
Through swift accomplishment, practitioners of mantra obtain renown;
through delay, they acquire wealth by making their great volume of ritual activity famous.
Those who extend comfort to those in comfort and life to those suffering in misery, acting for their benefit— they are indeed blessed practitioners of mantras.

*VAR: 12b em: sukhe sukhiṣu yāvad ajñānato maunam ācāro vā vilakṣaṇas / tāvan māhātmyarūpeṇa paryavasyati māntrike // NKv_13 //* As long as one remains silent out of ignorance regarding happiness among those who are happy, or behaves in a manner that is unconventional, so long does that [ignorance] culminate in the form of greatness for the practitioner of mantras.
Having analyzed the movements [of the planets], the results for kings must be declared by astrologers,
since a thorough knowledge of the movements of the planets is essential for them.
By saying "son" when asked about the father, and "daughter" when asked about the mother,
an astrologer who speaks thus regarding inquiries concerning the womb shall be victorious.
When asked about one's lifespan, astrologers should declare a long life;
for those who live are highly esteemed, whereas once dead, whom will they ask again?
Astrologers must declare everything as being endowed with both alternatives, everything as being limited by both times, and everything as if it were mixed.
Astrologers who claim that the poor will obtain wealth and the wealthy will gain even more wealth should be accepted by people in every respect.
Betel for a gain of a hundred, and a meal for a thousand—
these are the constant reproaches leveled against astrologers when their predictions go astray.
Even the entire earth, bounded by the oceans, must be searched;
for there is not even a space of a single cubit that is devoid of those skilled in astrology.
Some understand the lunar mansions (*vāra*), some the planets (*graha*), and some the constellations (*ṛkṣa*);
those who understand all three are themselves the equals of Bṛhaspati.
These three— interpreters of omens, dreamers, and [those who serve] the deities—
are the natural enemies created for astrologers.
For beings who are healthy or afflicted with incurable diseases, there is nothing [to be gained];
it is the timid and those with chronic illnesses who are the cause of fortune for physicians.

One should not show excessive composure toward the patient, nor should one display excessive fear; there should be no giving of medicine at the beginning out of a lack of concern, nor at the end out of despair.
Medicine may be taken according to one's desire, but one should declare that wholesome diet is difficult;
health results from the greatness of the physician, whereas its opposite results from unwholesome conduct.
The causes, the names of diseases, what is wholesome and unwholesome, and the methods of treatment—all this will be taught by women in the house of the patient. (NKv 26)
While diseases are spreading and living beings are dying,
physicians gradually gain proficiency in the true nature of those diseases.
Physicians desire to initiate [a treatment] at the beginning for the sake of setting it in motion, in the middle for the sake of the medicine, and at the end for the sake of gaining great respect.
While physicians are longing [for a patient], having finally found a sick person after a long time,
his heirs, astrologers, and even exorcists spring forth.
At the onset of illness there is consolation; in its middle stage, some expenditure of wealth;
gradually, a lack of concern during recovery; and once bathed and cured, one no longer visits the physician.
Astrology, mastery of mantras, medical practice, and skill in flattery—each one leads to the acquisition of wealth; however, the conjunction of two or three is rare indeed.
Falsehood, flattery, and the acquisition of great wealth—this is one thing;
truth and learning—this is another combination that brings about poverty.
Poets, who are like servants with handfuls of rice for the modest, sweep away all cowardice, ill-breeding, meanness, and lack of discernment.
Poets intent on praising do not depend upon any cause; even when there is nothing to praise, their tongues quiver with fervor.
Poets praise what has already been praised; they do not perceive qualities for themselves.
There is a certain bee named Kīta—what description could there possibly be of him?
A single poem is sufficient for men to provide for a village, a horse, an elephant,
and ultimately even for food, clothing, and betel.
The other Brahman, known as Sound, refined through its composition,
is sold by some, while by others it is used in vain.
Those people who, despite having obtained eloquence, describe mere semblances of men, are like those who,
having obtained the wish-fulfilling cow, employ her for plowing.
Praising those who merely appear to be men, prattling on in various ways,
how can these poets— proponents of the doctrine that the ultimate is desire— cross over?
If Śaṅkara is described, then that [composition] is superior even to meditative absorption— whether it be in its composition, its mention, or its suggested meaning— for one whose mind is composed.
Relatives,
the wife, the sister, her parents-in-law, and the brother-in-law—
these five others are created by Kali as the vital breaths of living beings.
Sons-in-law, nephews, maternal uncles, and wives' relatives—
though unknown to householders, they devour them in the home like rats.
The mother is the strength of the maternal uncle; the daughter is the strength of the son-in-law;
the wife is the strength of the father-in-law; and the guest himself is his own strength.
The crookedness of the son-in-law lasts as long as the childhood of the brother-in-law;
when he awakens, there is straightforwardness, but once he is fully awake, there is flight.
An elder wife, a young brother-in-law, a mother-in-law who acts with independence,
and a father-in-law living abroad— such is the succession of fortunes for a son-in-law.
Adorned with ornaments, perfumes, and vessels, and fondling her sons,
the daughter-in-law departs after visiting the house but once, leaving it polished clean.
The housewife tells her own kin that they eat dry food and in moderation, yet she describes those on her husband's side as gluttonous, drinkers of milk, and even thieves.
Two wives blessed with sons and a sister deprived of a husband—
this is the yoga known as "Unceasing Quarrel" for householders.
Two wives, many sons, poverty, the onset of disease,
and aged parents— each one of these is greater than hell.
When remembered, the limbs fail; when seen, wisdom perishes. Oh, how great is this being called "debt" by creditors! (NKv 50)
For even Death awaits the time of death for living beings;
however, there is no fixed rule regarding the time for one who has attained the supreme goal.
We see no fangs in your mouth, nor a noose in your cupped hands;
yet, upon merely seeing the Supreme Debtor, our minds are thus agitated.
Conciliation is the remedy for an enemy, medicine is the remedy for all diseases,
and meditation on the Conqueror of Death is the remedy for death; but for poverty, there is no remedy at all.
It provides strength for movement, endures both cold and heat,
kindles the fire within the stomach, and is the supreme medicine for poverty.
Poverty, like a royal command, urges one toward begging, even as one's speech falters, one's vision blurs, and one's feet falter.
They wither through hatred for the king, and they wither even when not [otherwise] decreed. *VAR. 55b: em: visaṃsthulau; ed: visaṃsphuṭau*
For those enriched by the power of non-possessiveness, even a stone is eventually worn away.
Neither thieves, nor informers, nor heirs, nor kings shall prevail over him, if he awakens to the truth; for even sovereignty is better than wretchedness.
When fortune has arrived even slightly, it reveals one's ego, incites thieves, and emboldens kinsmen. (NKv 58)
Those wealthy people who constantly mock the wise are themselves mocked when their fortune is even slightly neglected.
The perception of authority in hymns, the perception of divinity in oneself,
and the perception of mere insects in human beings— this is the fruit of newly acquired fortune.
They ask even while listening; they do not understand even while looking.
These wealthy men regard their own insults as hymns of praise.
Blinded by the intoxication of wealth, having made secret agreements with one another,
those standing at their sides laugh freely like children, madmen, or ghosts.
Though he is constantly praised by those worthy of praise and served by those worthy of service,
even so, the wealthy man neither fears nor feels shame.
The possession by a spirit lasts but a moment; the intoxication from wine lasts but a watch of the night; but the intoxication of wealth among fools persists as long as the body endures.
Prosperity, having exerted itself for a month or half a month, ceases;
but the transformation initiated by it persists eternally, like the odor of garlic.
Intoxication from *kodrava* grain resides in the throat; intoxication from betel resides in the heart;
but the intoxication of wealth pervades every limb, even in the presence of one's children and wife.
Let intoxication prevail wherever there was or is prosperity;
yet how could this [intoxication] descend even into a noble family like leprosy or epilepsy?
They teach the scriptures, treat scholars as mere straw, and cause them to forget their own lineage—all for five or six cowries in hand. (NKv 68)
Let the wealthy man support his dependents or give what is due to those who seek it;
as long as there is the condition of being a petitioner, the world will not tolerate [the withholding of gifts].
For the burden of wealth in the world is borne only by the slanderers themselves;
how else could they strive to lighten it for others than by doing so for themselves?
What benefit is provided by kings to a slanderer in proportion to his labor?
Yama will surely pamper him with double or even triple [recompense].
At Gokarṇa and at Bhadrakarṇa, recitation destroys evil deeds;
at Rājakarṇa, recitation immediately destroys all karmas.
They desire nothing for their own sake, nor are they impelled by anyone;
whether wicked or virtuous, they engage in the welfare of others equally.
For a vulture perched above one's house may lead to misfortune after some time,
but a wicked person standing near one's home leads to immediate misfortune for embodied beings.
For those possessed by greed, dry fasting among religious practices, fasting among medicines, and the sacrifice of recitation among sacrifices are what is pleasing. (NKv 75)
Just as one who lacks wealth is anxious, wondering what a creditor might say;
even so, a greedy person is anxious, wondering what he might be asked for.
The greedy ones directly realize the entire meaning of the treatise on hospitality,
for they regard even a single morsel of alms as being like Mount Meru.
For the wealth-guarding piśāca gives when his master is present;
yet the wealth-greedy piśāca does not wish to give to anyone at all.
Givers are sought by those who desire wealth, while seekers in turn are sought by givers;
through this mutual exchange of agent and object, oh, how great is the disparity between the low and the high!
"Since there would be no protector for an object if one were not oneself present," having thus determined, the greedy person eats [the object] himself by some means.
One who is about to set out should enter [the house], and one who wishes to remain should stay for a long time as a guest; thus, day by day, he should scatter various obstacles. NKv_81 //
In this world, according to the righteous, one [coin] is given to a learned woman, ten to a poet, a hundred to an actor, a thousand to a hypocrite, but nothing at all to a Vedic scholar (śrotriya).
Having properly propitiated the one who brings things together, one should maintain supreme detachment;
for worldly objects remain successful only so long as fickleness is concealed.
On one side are all the scriptures, and on the other side is a single piece of Tulasī wood;
if one must say something, it is said that in reality, Tulasī is supreme.
Or perhaps Vāhaṭa forgot this while reciting the qualities of Tulasī:
the two qualities of "deluding the world" and "bestowing wealth."
A loincloth, smearing oneself with ashes, a garland of darbha grass and rudrākṣa beads,
silence, and sitting alone— these are the six means of livelihood for fools.
Dwelling at sacred fords, being renowned, and having died as a teacher—
these modes of livelihood through teaching should be praised by those seeking wealth.
When there is a lapse in the mantra, the tradition [is the answer]; when the ritual application is corrupted, the usage;
and when there is improper conduct, the local custom—this is the established reply for those who inquire.
Just as many people know, and just as they will speak regarding a donor, so should one practice the Dharma in its entirety; one should not perform anything in vain.
Always having a rosary in hand, closing one's eyes from time to time,
and the constant proclamation that "all is Brahman"— these are the causes for immediate conviction.
Dwelling by a river until midday, worshiping deities in public assemblies,
and always wearing clean clothes— this is the very life of hypocrisy.
The daily ritual is as long as there is union with the Seer;
everything is abbreviated until the Seer is no longer perceived.
For one whose tears of joy and horripilation are subject to his own will, what need is there for other means? All kings are his servants.
When punished, the wicked act perversely; when pampered, they do so even more. Therefore, it is right to dismiss the wicked from afar.
For those of wicked intellect, non-giving or even a slight gift given with some provocation is their nature;
yet a complete gift is a cause for enmity and they cease [giving]. (NKv 95)
Not associating with the wicked is superior; conversely, association with them leads to envy.
Furthermore, the practice of forming kinship through offspring serves only one's own ruin.
If these four— lack of kinship, lack of knowledge, malice, and poverty— should meet together, then even to that direction, salutation, salutation!
The Creator fashioned the heart of the wicked for the holes of others, their ears for the reports concerning others, and their speech for the vital secrets of others.
Just as a scorpion with its venom clinging to its tail is dangerous to living beings,
so too is every moment of time terrible when even a tenth part of it is possessed by the Kali age.
Salutation to that Śrī Kāla, wherein the words of one's wife are the Vedas, wherein dharma is the means to achieve worldly ends, and wherein one's own intuition is the authority.
Granted that the entire world may be subject to the power of this time;
yet for those who have taken refuge in the Death of Death, what will time do to us?
This satire on the Kali age, titled *Rājāsthānānumodana*, was composed by the learned poet Nīlakaṇṭha for the delight of the wise.
Thus ends the *Kaliviḍambana* composed by Nīlakaṇṭha.
